docs.title: Daily sunscreen and skin aging

sources.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial
sources.by: Hughes MC et al. (Ann Intern Med)

docs.summary: In a 4.5-year randomized trial, adults who used broad-spectrum sunscreen every day showed no detectable increase in skin aging, and about 24% less aging than people who used it when they felt like it.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: In a 4.5-year randomized trial, adults who used broad-spectrum sunscreen every day showed no detectable increase in skin aging, and about 24% less aging than people who used it when they felt like it.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ on face, ears and neck, every morning, including cloudy days. Reapply when outdoors for long.
- It is the best-proven step for skin that looks younger and more even over the years.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Trial in adults under 55 in Australia, with high sun exposure. Measured by skin surface patterns.

docs.title: Reply to client inquiries fast

sources.title: The Short Life of Online Sales Leads
sources.by: Oldroyd JB, McElheran K, Elkington D (Harvard Business Review 89(3):28)

docs.summary: An audit of how companies answered web inquiries, published in Harvard Business Review in 2011, concluded that most companies do not respond nearly fast enough, and that the chance of turning an inquiry into a real conversation falls quickly as hours pass. For a small studio, replying first and personally is one of the cheapest edges available.

sections.text: An audit of how companies answered web inquiries, published in Harvard Business Review in 2011, concluded that most companies do not respond nearly fast enough, and that the chance of turning an inquiry into a real conversation falls quickly as hours pass. For a small studio, replying first and personally is one of the cheapest edges available.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Reply to every wedding or business inquiry within the hour during working hours, and the same day at the latest.
- Use a saved first reply that is still personal: thank them, use their names and date, ask one question, and suggest a call time.
- Push for a short call: it's where trust and booking happen.
- Follow up 2-3 times over a week if they go quiet; most people are busy, not uninterested.
- Track inquiries, reply time and bookings so you know your conversion rate.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The exact figures from the HBR article could not be verified from the full text, so none are quoted here. The research looked at B2B web leads from 2011, not wedding couples; treat the "reply fast" principle as well-supported practice, not a measured booking rate.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: The Knot's Real Weddings Study (10,474 U.S. couples married in 2025) put the average wedding videographer spend at $2,300. Spending ran $1,000 at the lower quartile, $1,900 at the median and $3,300 at the upper quartile. Regional averages ranged from about $2,100 (South, Southwest) to $3,000 (Mid-Atlantic). Price rises with hours of coverage, a second shooter, deliverables (social clips, cinematic feature, raw footage) and editing time.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Build 3 packages around the market: an entry package near the median, a core package near the upper quartile, and a premium package above it for couples who want more coverage and a cinematic film.
- Price on deliverables and hours, not on a day rate alone; list exactly what each tier includes.
- Most buyers anchor on the middle option, so make the middle tier the one you most want to sell (see [[comm-first-offer-anchoring]]).
- Raise prices as the portfolio and demand grow; a full calendar months ahead is a signal you are underpriced.
- Count all your time (calls, travel, editing, revisions) and self-employment tax when checking if a price is profitable (see [[wealth-self-employment-tax]]).

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: These are what couples reported spending, not what profitable videographers should charge. Survey averages hide wide local variation and differences in quality. Package and anchoring advice is practical business reasoning, not tested in this survey.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Alex Hormozi is an entrepreneur and investor. He opened a gym in 2013, turned his gym turnaround work into Gym Launch (licensed to thousands of gyms) and built Prestige Labs (supplements sold through the same gyms). He sold a majority stake in those businesses in 2021 (reported at $46.2M for 66%). With his wife Leila he runs Acquisition.com, which invests in profitable small companies, and he wrote $100M Offers and $100M Leads.

sections.heading: Main teachings
sections.text:
- Value Equation: perceived value goes up with the dream outcome and the perceived likelihood of achieving it, and goes down with time delay and effort and sacrifice. To raise value, fix the weakest of the four.
- Grand Slam Offer: stack bonuses, guarantees and scarcity so the offer is clearly worth more than the price, so you compete on value, not price.
- Risk reversal: guarantees lower the buyer's fear.
- Naming: make the offer name speak to a specific person, result and timeframe.
- Fund growth with customer cash flow; favor recurring and referral revenue.

sections.heading: Failures and mistakes
sections.text: He went broke twice early on, including after a partnership collapsed. Payment processors held his revenue for months because his business was flagged high-risk. After selling Gym Launch he said he felt poorer because the cash-flow engine was gone. He has publicly broken down his own content mistakes.

sections.heading: Evidence check
sections.text: His frameworks are expert opinion from his own industries (gyms, info products), not tested in controlled studies. The value equation lines up with well-known ideas in pricing and consumer psychology, but numbers like "10x value" are rules of thumb.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.text: Critics say the books simplify things, may not transfer to every industry, pay little attention to ethics and sustainability, and his free content funnels into expensive programs.

sections.heading: Practical application (videography business)
sections.text:
- Write one clear offer per niche: for example "a 60-second cinematic wedding highlight delivered in 14 days, or the edit is free".
- Raise perceived likelihood with proof: 3-5 sample films, testimonials, a clear process.
- Cut perceived effort: a simple booking link, a shot list template, one call to plan.
- Use referrals and recurring retainers (monthly content for gyms, restaurants, real estate agents) to smooth income.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Sources are secondary profiles and a study guide, not the books themselves; quoted figures (sale price, portfolio revenue) are as reported. Reading his books directly is a remaining gap.

docs.title: Negotiation: first offers as anchors

sources.title: First offers as anchors: the role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
sources.by: Galinsky AD, Mussweiler T (J Pers Soc Psychol)

docs.summary: In negotiation, the first number on the table tends to pull the final deal toward it. Galinsky and Mussweiler found that whoever made the first offer usually got the better outcome, and that the anchor's pull could be weakened when the other side focused on the first mover's alternatives or on their own target.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: In negotiation, the first number on the table tends to pull the final deal toward it. Galinsky and Mussweiler found that whoever made the first offer usually got the better outcome, and that the anchor's pull could be weakened when the other side focused on the first mover's alternatives or on their own target.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Quote first when you know the market: name a confident, well-justified package price (for example a premium wedding package), then explain the value.
- When a client anchors low, do not argue the number. Shift focus to the outcome and your package options, and restate your own target.
- Prepare your walk-away price and your best alternative before any call.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Lab negotiations with students; real deals involve relationships and repeat business.

docs.title: Focus and task switching (attention residue)

sources.title: Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks
sources.by: Leroy S (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 109(2):168-181)

docs.summary: In two experiments, Sophie Leroy found that when people switch tasks, part of their attention stays stuck on the previous one ("attention residue"), and performance on the next task drops. Leaving the first task unfinished made the residue worse; finishing it under some time pressure helped people let go and do better on the next task.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: In two experiments, Sophie Leroy found that when people switch tasks, part of their attention stays stuck on the previous one ("attention residue"), and performance on the next task drops. Leaving the first task unfinished made the residue worse; finishing it under some time pressure helped people let go and do better on the next task.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Work in single-task blocks (for example 60-90 minutes of editing) with notifications off and the phone in another room.
- Finish a clear chunk before switching, or write a one-line "next step" note so the brain can let go.
- Give tasks a deadline inside the block; mild time pressure helped people disengage.
- Batch email and messages into set times instead of checking between edits.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Lab experiments with short tasks; effect sizes in real long workdays are not established. The block lengths above are practical suggestions, not tested values.

docs.title: Setting goals that actually drive performance

sources.title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation. A 35-year odyssey
sources.by: Locke EA, Latham GP (American Psychologist)

docs.summary: Specific, difficult goals lead to better performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. The effect is strongest when the person is committed, gets feedback on progress, and has the ability and strategy for the task.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Specific, difficult goals lead to better performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals. The effect is strongest when the person is committed, gets feedback on progress, and has the ability and strategy for the task.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Make goals specific and measurable: "+15 lb lean by late February", "$10K/month from videography".
- Add feedback: weekly weigh-in average, monthly revenue check.
- For complex goals (building a business), set learning goals first ("test 3 offers this month") before outcome goals.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Very difficult goals without the skills to reach them can lead to shortcuts or burnout.

docs.title: How long habits take to form

sources.title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
sources.by: Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J (European Journal of Social Psychology)

sources.title: How long does it take to form a habit? (UCL news on Lally et al.)
sources.by: University College London

docs.summary: Habits do not form in 21 days. In a 12-week study of 96 people who picked a daily eating, drinking or exercise behavior, it took a median of 66 days for the behavior to become close to automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. Missing a single day did not meaningfully set people back.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Habits do not form in 21 days. In a 12-week study of 96 people who picked a daily eating, drinking or exercise behavior, it took a median of 66 days for the behavior to become close to automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. Missing a single day did not meaningfully set people back.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Automaticity rises quickly at first, then levels off.
- Simpler behaviors (drinking water) became automatic faster than harder ones (exercise).
- Same cue, same time, same place each day helped.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Expect about 2-3 months of conscious effort before a new routine feels automatic. Plan for it.
- Anchor the habit to a fixed cue: "after I brush my teeth in the morning, I read one chapter".
- Never miss twice: one missed day does not break a habit, two starts a new pattern.
- Start smaller than you think, then grow it once it is automatic.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Small, self-reported study; many participants dropped data. The median hides huge individual variation.

docs.title: If-then plans (implementation intentions)

sources.title: Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes
sources.by: Gollwitzer PM, Sheeran P (Advances in Experimental Social Psychology)

docs.summary: Turning a goal into a specific "if situation X, then I will do Y" plan makes people much more likely to follow through. A meta-analysis of 94 studies (over 8,000 people) found a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65) on goal attainment.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Turning a goal into a specific "if situation X, then I will do Y" plan makes people much more likely to follow through. A meta-analysis of 94 studies (over 8,000 people) found a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65) on goal attainment.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Write if-then plans for the moments you usually fail: "If it's 5:30 pm on a weekday, then I drive straight to the gym in my gym clothes."
- Plan for obstacles: "If I'm tempted to skip the meal prep Sunday, then I start with just cooking the rice."
- Make the "when" and "where" exact. Vague intentions are what fail.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Effects are smaller for very complex goals and when the underlying goal is weak.

docs.title: Why we procrastinate and how to beat it

sources.title: The nature of procrastination: a meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure
sources.by: Steel P (Psychological Bulletin)

docs.summary: Procrastination is mostly about motivation over time, not laziness. Steel's meta-analysis found the strongest predictors were how unpleasant the task feels, how far away the reward is, low confidence you can do it, and impulsiveness and distractibility.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Procrastination is mostly about motivation over time, not laziness. Steel's meta-analysis found the strongest predictors were how unpleasant the task feels, how far away the reward is, low confidence you can do it, and impulsiveness and distractibility.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Shrink the task until it is not aversive: "edit the first 30 seconds of the wedding film", not "edit the film".
- Bring the reward closer: set a near deadline, tell the client a date, reward yourself right after.
- Build confidence with quick wins first.
- Remove distractions during work blocks (phone in another room, one tab).

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Mostly correlational data from students and self-reports.

docs.title: Is willpower a limited tank? (ego depletion)
docs.conflicts: Earlier studies reported large depletion effects; large preregistered replications found effects close to zero.

sources.title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect
sources.by: Hagger MS et al. (Perspectives on Psychological Science)

docs.summary: The popular idea that willpower is a fuel tank that runs out with use is disputed. A preregistered replication across 23 labs and over 2,000 participants found an effect close to zero. Self-control is better built by designing your environment and routines than by trying to "save" willpower.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: The popular idea that willpower is a fuel tank that runs out with use is disputed. A preregistered replication across 23 labs and over 2,000 participants found an effect close to zero. Self-control is better built by designing your environment and routines than by trying to "save" willpower.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Remove decisions: lay out gym clothes, prep meals, keep junk food out of the house, phone outside the bedroom.
- Make the good choice the easy default and the bad choice inconvenient.
- Do not tell yourself you "used up" willpower; that belief itself may make you quit sooner.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The debate continues; some researchers argue the replication task was too weak. Treat "willpower tank" claims as unsupported, not as proven false.

Verse text checked against the World English Bible (public domain): - Philippians 4:6-7: "In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus." - Matthew 6

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text:
Scripture answers worry with prayer and trust, not denial. Verse text checked against the World English Bible (public domain):
- Philippians 4:6-7: "In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus."
- Matthew 6:33-34: "But seek first God's Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well. Therefore don't be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day's own evil is sufficient."
- 1 Peter 5:7: "casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you."

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- When anxious, name the specific worry and pray it out loud or on paper, including thanks for what is already good (Philippians 4:6).
- Put first things first each morning: prayer and Scripture before the phone (Matthew 6:33).
- Handle today's work and let tomorrow wait (Matthew 6:34); plan, then stop rehearsing.
- Pair faith with action: prayer does not replace doing the work or getting help.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: These verses are about trust and prayer, not a promise that feelings disappear instantly. Persistent anxiety that affects sleep, work or relationships is worth raising with a doctor or counselor; seeking help is consistent with faith.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Scripture treats discipline as part of following Christ, not as self-improvement for its own sake. Paul uses the athlete as a picture of the Christian life: training with purpose and self-control for a prize that lasts. Self-control is listed as a fruit of the Spirit, which means it grows from life with God, not from willpower alone.

sections.heading: Scripture (text)
sections.text:
- 1 Corinthians 9:24-25 (WEB): "Don't you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win. Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible."
- 1 Corinthians 9:26-27 (WEB): "I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air, but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected."
- Hebrews 12:11 (WEB) begins: "All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous;" and goes on to say that afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
- Galatians 5:22-23 lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit (read the passage at the link).
- Proverbs 25:28 compares a person without self-control to a city whose walls are broken down (read at the link).
- 2 Timothy 1:7 says God gave a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control (read at the link; some translations say "sound mind" or "discipline").

sections.heading: Context
sections.text:
- 1 Corinthians 9: Paul explains why he gives up his rights for the sake of the gospel. The athlete image is about purposeful self-denial for others and for an eternal prize, not about body image. Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, so readers knew athletes' training well.
- Hebrews 12: "discipline" there is God's fatherly training through hardship; it is the backdrop for enduring difficulty with hope.
- Galatians 5: self-control is the Spirit's fruit set against "the works of the flesh"; the contrast is about walking by the Spirit.

sections.heading: Interpretation (labeled)
sections.text: Across Christian traditions, these passages are read as calling believers to train habits (prayer, Scripture, work, the body) with eternal purpose, depending on God's grace rather than pride. Denominations differ on emphasis (for example, the role of spiritual disciplines vs grace), not on self-control being good.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Tie physical training to purpose: stewardship of the body and energy to serve others.
- Pair the gym habit with a small spiritual habit at the same time each day (for example reading one chapter before the first meal).
- When motivation is low, pray for self-control as fruit to grow, and keep the habit small rather than skipping it.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Exact quotes are from the public-domain World English Bible; other translations word verses differently. Historical notes on Corinth are standard background, not yet linked to a specific scholarly source here.

docs.title: Alcohol and muscle building

sources.title: Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis following a single bout of concurrent training
sources.by: Parr EB et al. (PLoS One)

docs.summary: Heavy drinking after training reduces muscle building. In a controlled study, a large amount of alcohol after exercise lowered muscle protein synthesis even when protein was eaten with it, though protein reduced the damage.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Heavy drinking after training reduces muscle building. In a controlled study, a large amount of alcohol after exercise lowered muscle protein synthesis even when protein was eaten with it, though protein reduced the damage.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Avoid heavy drinking on training days, especially after leg or upper sessions you care about.
- If drinking, keep it moderate, eat protein, hydrate, and do not let it cut sleep.
- Alcohol also adds empty calories and often causes next-day facial puffiness.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: One acute study of a large dose in a small group of men; light drinking was not tested.

docs.title: Daily steps and long-term health

sources.title: Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts
sources.by: Paluch AE et al. (Lancet Public Health)

docs.summary: More daily steps were linked to lower risk of death, with benefits leveling off around 8,000-10,000 steps a day for adults under 60 and 6,000-8,000 for older adults.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: More daily steps were linked to lower risk of death, with benefits leveling off around 8,000-10,000 steps a day for adults under 60 and 6,000-8,000 for older adults.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- 8,000-10,000 steps covers most of the health benefit. Higher counts are fine but burn more calories, which must be eaten back on a bulk.
- Walking is a low-fatigue way to stay fit without hurting recovery.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Observational data: association, not proof of cause.

sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
- Regulators flagged many compounded peptides over safety concerns (immune reactions, impurities, hard-to-characterize ingredients, too little human safety data). In 2023 the FDA placed a group of peptides in its "Category 2" (significant safety risks) list for compounding; in April 2026 it moved several peptides out of Category 2 pending an advisory committee review, which does not mean they are approved.
- Products sold online are not quality-controlled; contents and sterility are unknown.
- IGF-1 activity affects blood sugar; low blood sugar is a known risk of IGF-1 drugs.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- The app never gives doses, schedules, combinations or ways to use these products.
- If he uses or considers them: do it only under a qualified doctor's supervision, with bloodwork (including glucose) and an honest discussion of risks; stop and seek care for symptoms like shakiness, sweating, confusion or chest pain.
- The proven levers for muscle (hard progressive training, enough protein and calories, sleep, creatine) carry far more evidence.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Regulatory status changes; re-check by the review date. This is safety and status information, not medical advice.

docs.title: How much sleep adults need

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult (AASM and Sleep Research Society consensus)
sources.by: Watson NF et al. (J Clin Sleep Med)

docs.summary: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours a night for health. Sleeping less on a regular basis is linked with weight gain, worse mood and performance, impaired immunity and higher risk of several diseases. More than 9 hours may be appropriate for young adults, after sleep debt, or during illness.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours a night for health. Sleeping less on a regular basis is linked with weight gain, worse mood and performance, impaired immunity and higher risk of several diseases. More than 9 hours may be appropriate for young adults, after sleep debt, or during illness.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Treat 8 hours in bed as the training target, to get 7+ hours of actual sleep.
- Keep a consistent wake time, even on weekends; it anchors the body clock.
- Morning light, no caffeine within about 8 hours of bed, a cool dark room, and phones out of bed.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Consensus based on reviewing the evidence, mostly observational links rather than trials of sleep extension.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Caffeine reliably improves many types of performance, including strength and endurance. The ISSN reports benefits at about 3-6 mg per kg taken about an hour before, with lower amounts also helping some people. The cost is sleep: in a controlled study, a large dose (400 mg) even 6 hours before bed cut sleep by more than an hour.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Use the smallest amount that works and keep it at least 8 hours before bed for evening sleepers.
- Count all sources: coffee, pre-workout, energy drinks.
- If training in the evening, consider caffeine-free sessions to protect sleep, which matters more for growth.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Response varies with genetics and habitual intake. People with heart conditions, anxiety or high blood pressure should check with a doctor.

- Adjust calories by about 100-200 kcal only after 2-3 weeks of trend data.
- Track waist weekly: if the waist climbs fast while strength stalls, the surplus is too big.
- Keep protein about 1.6-2.2 g/kg and fill the rest with carbs to fuel training.

sections.heading: Limitations

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Protein supplementation increased gains in fat-free mass and strength from training.

- The effect is larger in trained lifters than beginners, and smaller with age.

- At 79 kg (175 lb): about 127 g/day covers most people; 175 g/day covers the high end. A 200 g target is safe for a healthy person but not required; extra calories may be better spent on carbs for training.
- Total daily protein matters most; food or shakes both count.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Most included trials were 6-24 weeks. Needs during a cut (calorie deficit) are higher; see the contest-prep review.

docs.summary: Brad Schoenfeld is one of the most published researchers on muscle hypertrophy. His reviews and meta-analyses on volume, frequency, load, rest and protein timing shape much of today's evidence-based bodybuilding advice.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Brad Schoenfeld is one of the most published researchers on muscle hypertrophy. His reviews and meta-analyses on volume, frequency, load, rest and protein timing shape much of today's evidence-based bodybuilding advice.

sections.heading: Main teachings
sections.text:
- Mechanical tension is the main driver of growth.
- Volume has a dose-response relationship with growth; about 10+ hard sets per muscle per week is a good baseline.
- With equal weekly volume, frequency matters little; training each muscle twice a week is a practical default.
- A wide range of loads builds muscle if sets are hard; heavy loads build more strength.
- Longer rests (2-3 minutes) help keep set quality high.

sections.heading: Evidence check
sections.text: His positions come from meta-analyses of controlled trials, the strongest evidence available in this field. Their limits: short studies, young subjects, and site-specific muscle measures.

sections.heading: Where experts disagree
sections.text: Researchers still debate how high volume should go before returns flatten, and how much stretch-position training adds.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text: Use his findings as the default rules for programming, then adjust to personal recovery, schedule and lagging muscles.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This profile covers his research positions, not biography details; those are not yet researched in this library.

sections.heading: Summary

sections.heading: Main teachings
sections.text:
- Natural lifters should gain and lose slowly: slow off-season gains limit fat, slow cuts protect muscle.
- High protein during a cut (relative to fat-free mass) helps keep muscle.
- Effort (reps in reserve) and progressive overload matter more than exotic techniques.
- Supplements are minor; creatine and caffeine are among the few with good support.

sections.heading: Evidence check
sections.text: His guidance is based on systematic reading of the evidence, but much of the bodybuilding-specific data are case studies and small samples; he flags these limits himself.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text: For a lean bulk: modest surplus, weekly average weight trend, protein about 1.6-2.2 g/kg, hard progressive training, and patience across months.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Profile based on two of his reviews; his books and later work are not yet researched in this library.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Greg Plitt (1977-2015) was a fitness model, trainer and motivational speaker from Maryland. He graduated from West Point (class of 2000), was Airborne and Ranger qualified and served five years as an Army Ranger. He then became one of the most-photographed fitness cover models (Muscle & Fitness, Men's Health, Men's Fitness and others), starred in Bravo's Work Out, and built a large following through intense motivational videos. He died on January 17, 2015, at 37, when he was struck by a train in Burbank, California, while filming a video.

sections.heading: Expertise and achievements
sections.text:
- Military leadership and physical training background (West Point, Rangers).
- Created the MFT28 ("Military Fitness Trainer") 28-day program published on Bodybuilding.com, plus stair challenges like "1044 Steps to Paradise".
- MET-Rx athlete team member; their 2012 Athlete of the Year.
- His physique was used as a body reference for Dr. Manhattan in Watchmen (2009).

sections.heading: Philosophy and teachings
sections.text:
- Training is a vehicle for character: every rep should mean something beyond looks.
- Do the hard things most people avoid; the difficult tasks are the least done and the most rewarding.
- Stay the course and keep focus; success compounds from consistent effort.
- Live so you can look back without regret, and ask how you want to be remembered.
- Take calculated risks rather than being ruled by fear.
- Build a personal brand by being genuinely yourself and using your personality to lift others.

sections.heading: Proven strategies (what holds up)
sections.text:
- High-effort sessions, consistency and accountability: these line up with the research on proximity to failure and habit formation.
- Military-style structure (set times, set routines) is a sound way to remove daily decision-making.

sections.heading: Failures and mistakes
sections.text: - His death came from filming near an active train line. Reported accounts say he may have tried to outrun the train; this is reported, not confirmed. The lesson that applies: intensity is not the same as taking unnecessary physical risks.

sections.heading: Evidence check
sections.text:
- His methods were coaching experience, not tested programs. Many of his workouts were very high volume and high intensity; that works for some, but research shows growth comes from enough hard sets, progression and recovery, not maximal punishment.
- No published data show MFT28 outcomes. Treat it as one structured program among many.

sections.heading: Where his advice may be outdated
sections.text: - Some period fitness media favored extreme cuts for shoots. For a lean bulk, slow gain and sleep matter more than photo-shoot leanness.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Use his mindset as fuel for consistency and standards (show up, finish the set, do the hard thing first), and use evidence-based programming for the actual sets, reps and food.
- Pair motivation with systems: a scheduled session, a logged workout and a measured weekly result.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Biographical facts come from an encyclopedia with citations and a publisher tribute; his teachings are paraphrased from those sources, not from a full review of his video archive. More profile research on his videos and nutrition views is still a gap.

sources.title: Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises

docs.summary: Moderate cardio does not stop you from building muscle, but a lot of it, especially running, can blunt gains in size and strength. The interference grew with more frequent and longer cardio sessions; cycling interfered less than running.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Moderate cardio does not stop you from building muscle, but a lot of it, especially running, can blunt gains in size and strength. The interference grew with more frequent and longer cardio sessions; cycling interfered less than running.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- On a bulk, keep hard cardio to about 2-3 sessions a week of 20-30 minutes; walking (like his step goal) has little interference.
- Separate hard cardio from leg training by several hours, or do it on another day.
- Eat back what cardio burns: 15,000 steps a day can add several hundred calories of expenditure.
- Keep some conditioning for heart health and work capacity; the goal is managing dose, not avoiding cardio.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: 2012 meta-analysis of mostly short studies; newer studies suggest interference may be smaller in well-fed, well-recovered trainees.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Muscle grows when its fibers are exposed to enough mechanical tension, often enough, with enough food and recovery. Schoenfeld's 2010 review proposed three drivers: mechanical tension, metabolic stress (the "burn" and pump) and muscle damage. Since then, most researchers treat mechanical tension on working fibers as the main driver; stress and damage are side effects that may contribute a little at most.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Tension on the muscle fibers, especially when sets get hard enough that most motor units are recruited, signals the muscle to add protein.
- Soreness and damage are not required for growth. Chasing soreness can cut into how much quality work you can do the following days.
- The pump is a sign of blood flow and metabolites, not proof a set was productive.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Judge a session by hard sets close to failure with good technique and a full range of motion, not by soreness or pump.
- Progress the load or reps over weeks so the tension stays high as you get stronger.
- Recovery (sleep, protein, a calorie surplus when bulking) is where the growth is actually built.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This is a narrative review from 2010. Its three-mechanism model is a framework, not a proven formula, and the weight given to each mechanism has shifted with newer studies.

docs.title: Strength training and injury prevention

sources.title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries
sources.by: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB (Br J Sports Med)
sources.kind: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs

docs.summary: Strength training is one of the best-supported ways to prevent sports injuries. In a meta-analysis of randomized trials, strength training cut sports injuries to under a third, while static stretching showed no protective effect.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Strength training is one of the best-supported ways to prevent sports injuries. In a meta-analysis of randomized trials, strength training cut sports injuries to under a third, while static stretching showed no protective effect.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Warm up with lighter sets of the first lift instead of long static stretching.
- Progress loads gradually (small jumps, logged), keep 1-2 reps in reserve on heavy compound lifts, and use controlled technique.
- Train the back and rear delts at least as much as pressing to balance the shoulders.
- Sharp or worsening joint pain is a stop signal: swap the exercise and see a physio if it persists.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The trials were in sports populations, not specifically bodybuilders, and injury definitions varied.

docs.title: Heavy vs light weights and rep ranges

sources.title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training
sources.by: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW (J Strength Cond Res)

sources.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
sources.by: Lopez P et al. (Med Sci Sports Exerc)

docs.summary: Light, moderate and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure. Heavy loads build more maximal strength. So the rep range is mostly a practical choice: pick what lets you train hard, safely and consistently.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Light, moderate and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure. Heavy loads build more maximal strength. So the rep range is mostly a practical choice: pick what lets you train hard, safely and consistently.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Schoenfeld 2017: low-load (about 60% of 1RM or less) and high-load training produced similar hypertrophy when sets went to failure; high loads won for 1RM strength.
- Lopez 2021: across low, moderate and high loads, hypertrophy was similar; strength favored heavier loads.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Use about 5-30 reps per set for growth. Most sets in the 6-15 range are efficient: heavy enough to progress, not so many reps that fatigue and discomfort end the set early.
- Keep heavier work (about 4-8 reps) on compound lifts if you also want strength.
- Very high-rep sets (20-30) are fine for joints-friendly isolation work but are uncomfortable and easy to stop short of failure.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: "Close to failure" matters: light sets stopped far from failure grow less. Most studies are in untrained or recreationally trained people over short periods.

docs.summary: Exercises that load a muscle while it is stretched tend to grow it more than versions that load it shortened. Two well-run trials show this: seated leg curls (hips bent, hamstrings long) beat lying leg curls, and overhead triceps extensions beat pushdowns for triceps growth.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Exercises that load a muscle while it is stretched tend to grow it more than versions that load it shortened. Two well-run trials show this: seated leg curls (hips bent, hamstrings long) beat lying leg curls, and overhead triceps extensions beat pushdowns for triceps growth.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Maeo 2021: 12 weeks of seated leg curls produced clearly more hamstring growth than lying leg curls.
- Maeo 2023: overhead elbow extensions produced substantially more triceps growth than the same work with arms at the sides, including in the lateral and medial heads.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Prefer stretch-loaded options: seated over lying leg curls, overhead extensions in addition to pushdowns, incline curls or preacher curls for biceps, deep-stretch flyes, deficit or full-depth calf raises, Romanian deadlifts.
- Use a full range of motion and control the stretched part of the rep instead of bouncing.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Small samples of untrained or lightly trained adults. Not every muscle has been tested, and "lengthened partials" alone are still emerging evidence.

docs.title: Progressive overload (adding weight or reps)

sources.title: Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations
sources.by: Plotkin D et al. (PeerJ)

docs.summary: To keep growing, the work has to get harder over time. Adding weight and adding reps at the same weight both work: in Plotkin 2022, progressing load or progressing reps produced similar muscle growth over 8 weeks, with small differences in strength measures.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: To keep growing, the work has to get harder over time. Adding weight and adding reps at the same weight both work: in Plotkin 2022, progressing load or progressing reps produced similar muscle growth over 8 weeks, with small differences in strength measures.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Progressing reps (same weight, more reps) gave similar hypertrophy to progressing load.
- Progressing load was a little better for 1RM squat strength; rep progression was a little better for muscular endurance.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Use double progression: choose a rep range (for example 8-12). When you hit the top of the range on all sets with good form, add the smallest weight jump and start again at the bottom.
- Log every working set (the app does this) and aim to beat the last session by a rep or a small amount of weight.
- If a lift stalls for 3 sessions: check sleep and food first, then swap the variation or reduce fatigue, before adding more volume.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: One 8-week trial in trained-but-not-elite men. Long-term progress also depends on eating enough, sleep and exercise selection.

docs.title: How close to failure to train (RIR)

sources.title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.by: Refalo MC et al. (Sports Med)

sources.title: Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.by: Robinson ZP et al. (Sports Med)

docs.summary: Sets need to be hard to grow muscle, but going all the way to failure on every set is not necessary. Growth tends to rise as sets get closer to failure, while strength gains are much less sensitive to it.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Sets need to be hard to grow muscle, but going all the way to failure on every set is not necessary. Growth tends to rise as sets get closer to failure, while strength gains are much less sensitive to it.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Refalo 2023: training to failure and stopping short produced similar hypertrophy overall; the authors suggest stopping a few reps short is enough if sets are genuinely hard.
- Robinson 2024: hypertrophy increased as estimated reps in reserve went down (closer to failure); strength did not show the same relationship.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Most working sets: 0-3 reps in reserve (you could do 0-3 more clean reps).
- Take the last set of isolation and machine exercises to failure; keep heavy barbell squats, deadlifts and bench a rep or two short for safety and recovery.
- Check yourself: if you often "had 5 more reps", the set was too easy to count as a hard set.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: People are bad at guessing reps in reserve, especially on high-rep sets. Most data are short-term and in less-trained lifters.

docs.title: Rest time between sets

sources.title: Longer Interset Rest Periods Enhance Muscle Strength and Hypertrophy in Resistance-Trained Men
sources.by: Schoenfeld BJ et al. (J Strength Cond Res)

docs.summary: Short rest (about 1 minute) can reduce how much work you get done in later sets. In trained men, 3-minute rests produced more strength and more growth in some measures than 1-minute rests over 8 weeks.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: Short rest (about 1 minute) can reduce how much work you get done in later sets. In trained men, 3-minute rests produced more strength and more growth in some measures than 1-minute rests over 8 weeks.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Rest about 2-3 minutes on heavy compound lifts, 1-2 minutes on isolation work.
- Rest until you can repeat a quality set, not by a strict clock. If reps crash on set two, rest longer.
- Short on time: use supersets of non-competing muscles (for example biceps with triceps) instead of cutting rest on big lifts.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Single 8-week trial with a small sample. Volume was matched by sets, not by total work, which partly explains the result.

docs.title: Side delts and shoulder width (lateral raises)

sources.title: Dumbbell versus cable lateral raises for lateral deltoid hypertrophy: an experimental study
sources.by: Larsen S, Wolf M, Schoenfeld BJ, et al. (Frontiers in Physiology 16)

In an 8-week within-person trial, 24 trained lifters did 5 sets of lateral raises to failure twice a week, one arm with cables and the other with dumbbells. Lateral delt thickness grew about 3-5% and the two tools produced essentially the same growth (Bayesian analysis favored "no difference").

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: The side (lateral) deltoid is what makes shoulders look wider from the front, so it drives the V-taper. In an 8-week within-person trial, 24 trained lifters did 5 sets of lateral raises to failure twice a week, one arm with cables and the other with dumbbells. Lateral delt thickness grew about 3-5% and the two tools produced essentially the same growth (Bayesian analysis favored "no difference"). Pick the version you can do with good form and progress over time.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Treat side delts as their own muscle: presses mostly train the front delts, so add direct lateral raises.
- About 10-20 hard sets of lateral raises per week, spread over 2-3 sessions, fits the general volume research (see [[phys-weekly-volume]]).
- Cables or dumbbells both work. Cables keep tension near the bottom; dumbbells are simpler. Machines are fine too.
- Take sets close to failure with controlled reps (see [[phys-proximity-to-failure]]); add reps first, then load.
- Track shoulder width with the tape (shoulders measurement) and front photos every 2-4 weeks, since growth here is slow.
- Lower body fat makes shoulder width look more pronounced; leanness and delt size work together.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: One 8-week study in 24 people measured with ultrasound; small and short. It compared tools, not the best weekly volume for delts specifically. The volume range is borrowed from general hypertrophy research, not delt-specific trials.

docs.title: How often to train each muscle (frequency)

sources.title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.by: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW (Sports Med)

sources.title: How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy?
sources.by: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Krieger J (J Sports Sci)

docs.summary: When weekly sets are the same, training a muscle once, twice or three times a week grows it about equally. Frequency matters mainly as a tool to fit in enough quality volume: splitting 16 sets into two or three sessions keeps each set fresher than doing them all in one day.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: When weekly sets are the same, training a muscle once, twice or three times a week grows it about equally. Frequency matters mainly as a tool to fit in enough quality volume: splitting 16 sets into two or three sessions keeps each set fresher than doing them all in one day.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- 2016 meta-analysis: training a muscle at least twice a week produced more growth than once, but many of those studies also differed in volume.
- 2019 meta-analysis, volume-equated: no meaningful difference in hypertrophy across frequencies.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Hit each muscle about twice a week as a default. Split very high weekly volume across more sessions.
- Pick the split you will actually follow. Push/pull/legs twice a week, upper/lower four days, or full body three days all work.
- For a lagging muscle, adding a third short session with a few hard sets is an easy way to add volume without long workouts.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Studies are mostly 6-12 weeks and in young adults. Very high frequencies (5-6 times a week per muscle) are less studied.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Small left-right differences are normal. Bring a lagging side up by giving it equal, honest work, not by doing extra sets only on that side forever.
- Use single-arm or single-leg versions (dumbbell press, one-arm cable row, split squats) for some of the work so the stronger side can't take over.
- Start each unilateral set with the weaker side and match its reps with the stronger side.
- Keep the big bilateral lifts if you want to get stronger at them, because strength is specific.
- Track it: arm and thigh tape measurements left vs right and photo scores (arm_left / arm_right) every few weeks.
- A large or sudden difference with pain, weakness or numbness is a reason to see a clinician, not to train harder.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Only 9 studies were included and the hypertrophy estimate had very wide uncertainty. No trial directly tested the best way to correct an existing asymmetry; the advice above is practical reasoning from the specificity finding.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Chaves 2020: 47 untrained men, 8 weeks, once a week. Incline-only pressing increased upper-chest thickness more than flat-only or a mix; other chest regions did not differ.
- EMG studies generally show more upper-chest activity on incline angles, but EMG does not reliably predict growth.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Put an incline press (barbell, dumbbell, Smith or machine, roughly 30-45 degrees) first on at least one chest day, for 3-4 hard sets.
- Add low-to-high cable flyes or incline flyes for stretch under load.
- Keep total chest volume and progressive overload in place; angle choice only shifts where the growth goes.
- Check progress with photos from the same angle and light every 4-6 weeks.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Single small longitudinal trial in untrained men training once a week; results in trained lifters may be smaller. Upper-chest shape is also influenced by genetics and body fat.

sections.heading: Conflicting evidence
sections.text: Acute swelling data suggested flat bench may hit the upper chest similarly. Reviewers consider the longitudinal data more informative but still thin.

Schoenfeld's 2017 meta-analysis found a graded dose-response: about 10 or more weekly sets per muscle produced more growth than fewer. Newer analyses suggest the benefit keeps rising with volume but with diminishing returns, so each extra set buys less.

sections.heading: Key findings
sections.text:
- Schoenfeld 2017: each added weekly set was associated with a small extra increase in muscle size; 10+ sets a week beat fewer than 5.
- Baz-Valle 2022: roughly 12-20 weekly sets per muscle looked like a sensible range for trained people; going higher did not reliably add more.
- Pelland 2024 (preprint, not yet peer reviewed when checked): growth kept increasing with volume with clear diminishing returns, while strength gains plateaued sooner.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Count only hard sets (within about 0-3 reps of failure) for the muscle that is actually the main mover.
- Start a lagging muscle at about 10-12 hard sets a week and add 2-4 sets when progress stalls and recovery is good, rather than jumping to very high volume.
- If performance drops for 2+ weeks, joints ache, or sleep is poor, cut volume before adding more.
- For a bulk with limited time, put extra sets on the 1-3 muscles you most want to bring up, and keep the rest at maintenance-to-moderate volume.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Most studies last 6-12 weeks, use young men, and measure muscle thickness in one spot. Set counting rules differ (for example whether bench press counts for triceps). Individual response varies a lot.

- If one debt has a much higher rate (for example a credit card at 25%+), attack that first.
- Never miss minimum payments; set autopay.

sections.text: The debt data came from people in a settlement program; dollar repayment and accounts closed were highly correlated. General education only.

sections.text: Even small amounts of easy-to-reach savings make a big difference in avoiding debt spirals. When the CFPB launched its savings initiative, it noted that 40% of Americans could not cover a $400 emergency from their own savings. A starter cushion comes before investing aggressively.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- Step 1: a starter fund of about one month of essentials in a separate high-yield savings account.
- Step 2: build toward 3-6 months of essentials; aim for the higher end with irregular self-employment income (videography).
- Automate a transfer on payday so saving happens before spending.
- Use the fund only for true emergencies and refill it first afterward.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This is general education, not personal financial advice. The 3-6 month range is a common planning convention, not a law.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: An index fund is a mutual fund or ETF that tries to match a market index such as the S&P 500 instead of picking stocks. The SEC explains that passive management can lower costs, and that between two funds with the same holdings, the cheaper one generally returns more, though not every index fund is cheap. S&P's SPIVA scorecard tracks how active managers do against their benchmark: in the first half of 2025, 54% of active large-cap U.S. funds trailed the S&P 500 (65% in full-year 2024), and the institutional scorecard reported at least 80% of equity funds underperformed over 10 years to the end of 2024.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- For most long-term investing, a low-cost broad index fund is a sensible default: check the expense ratio before buying.
- Invest money you won't need for at least 5 years; short-term money belongs in the emergency fund (see [[wealth-emergency-fund]]).
- Automate a monthly contribution and don't try to time the market.
- Prefer tax-advantaged accounts first where they fit (see [[wealth-roth-ira]]).

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: General education, not personal financial advice. Index funds still lose value when markets fall and can't dodge declines. SPIVA results vary by year and category (mid- and small-cap managers did better in early 2025), and past results do not guarantee future returns.

sections.heading: Practical application
sections.text:
- At 20 with income well under the phase-out, a Roth IRA is a strong first retirement account: decades of tax-free growth.
- You need earned income (videography income counts) to contribute; you cannot put in more than you earned.
- Inside the Roth, buy low-cost index funds (see [[wealth-index-funds]]); an IRA is just the account, not the investment.
- Build the emergency fund first (see [[wealth-emergency-fund]]) and set money aside for self-employment tax (see [[wealth-self-employment-tax]]).
- As the business grows, self-employed plans (SEP-IRA, Solo 401(k)) allow much higher contributions; ask a CPA which fits.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: General education, not personal tax or financial advice. Limits change every year; this doc must be re-checked when the IRS publishes 2027 limits (late 2026). Withdrawal rules (five-year rule, age 59½, exceptions) are in IRS Publication 590-B and are not covered here.

- Track business expenses (camera gear, software, mileage) to reduce taxable profit.
